questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What is accommodation with respect to vision?

(ii) Describe how mammals regulate the amount of light entering the eye. *[10 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Accommodation** *(2 marks)*

**Accommodation** is the **ability of the eye to change the focal length (refractive power) of the lens** so that **light from objects at different distances is focused sharply on the retina**. It is done by changing the **shape of the lens** (thicker and more curved for near objects, thinner and flatter for distant objects) by the **ciliary muscles** acting on the **suspensory ligaments**.

**(ii) Regulation of the amount of light entering the eye** *(8 marks)*

The main control is the **pupil (iris) reflex**, an involuntary reflex that adjusts the size of the **pupil**. The **iris** has two sets of muscles: **circular (sphincter) muscles** and **radial muscles**.

- **In bright light:**
  1. Photoreceptors (rods and cones) in the **retina** are stimulated strongly.
  2. **Impulses** pass along the **optic nerve** to the **midbrain**.
  3. **Motor impulses** pass along **parasympathetic fibres** (oculomotor nerve) to the iris.
  4. The **circular muscles contract** and the **radial muscles relax**, so the pupil **constricts**.
  5. **Less light enters**, which prevents **damage and bleaching** of the retina and gives a sharper image.
- **In dim light:** the **radial muscles contract** (sympathetic fibres) and the circular muscles relax, so the pupil **dilates** and **more light enters**, giving better vision.
- It is a **negative feedback** reflex: the response corrects the stimulus and keeps the light on the retina within a suitable range.

**Other mechanisms:** the **eyelids, eyelashes and eyebrows** (blinking and screwing up the eyes in very bright light); the **black pigment (melanin) in the choroid** absorbs excess light and stops reflection inside the eye; and **dark adaptation** (change in the amount of visual pigment in rods and cones) adjusts sensitivity over a longer time.

*Diagram to draw:* the iris in bright and dim light (circular and radial muscles labelled) or the pupil reflex arc (retina, optic nerve, brain, oculomotor nerve, iris muscles).

questions.enonce_markdown: How color blindness brought about in man? *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Red-green colour blindness is an inherited, sex-linked recessive condition.**

1. The genes coding for the **visual pigments (opsins) of the red-sensitive and green-sensitive cones** are on the **X chromosome**. A **recessive allele ($X^b$)** gives a **defective or absent pigment** in one type of cone, so the person **cannot distinguish red from green**.
2. A **male (XY)** has **only one X chromosome**, so a single recessive allele ($X^bY$) is enough to cause the condition. A **female (XX)** must have **two** recessive alleles ($X^bX^b$), so colour blindness is **much more common in men** (about 8 per cent) than in women (about 0.5 per cent).
3. A **woman with one recessive allele ($X^BX^b$) is a carrier** with normal vision; she passes the allele to **half of her sons**, who are colour blind, and to half of her daughters, who are carriers. A colour-blind man cannot pass it to his sons (they get his Y chromosome); all his daughters are carriers.

*Cross:* carrier mother $X^BX^b$ $\times$ normal father $X^BY$ gives $X^BX^B$ (normal girl), $X^BX^b$ (carrier girl), $X^BY$ (normal boy), $X^bY$ (colour-blind boy).

(Colour blindness can also be **acquired**, by damage to the retina or optic nerve; a rare blue-yellow type is carried on an autosome.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Differentiate between rods and cones. *[6 marks]* *(2, 8, 4, 6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Feature | Rods | Cones |
|---|---|---|
| **Shape of the outer segment** | Long and **rod-shaped** | Short and **cone-shaped** |
| **Visual pigment** | **Rhodopsin** (visual purple), one type | **Iodopsin**, **three types** (sensitive to red, green and blue light) |
| **Sensitivity to light** | **Very sensitive**: work in **dim light** (night vision) | **Less sensitive**: work only in **bright light** |
| **Type of vision** | **Black and white** (no colour) | **Colour vision** |
| **Visual acuity** | **Low**: many rods connect to **one bipolar neurone** (convergence), so detail is poor | **High**: in the fovea, **one cone to one bipolar neurone**, so fine detail is seen |
| **Distribution on the retina** | Absent from the fovea, **abundant at the periphery** | **Concentrated at the fovea** (yellow spot), few at the periphery |
| **Number** | About 120 million | About 6 million |
